stem: A 55-year-old man develops a platelet count drop from 220,000 to 85,000/mm³ five days after starting unfractionated heparin for a DVT. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
rationale: This presentation is consistent with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Heparin must be stopped and replaced with a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban. Warfarin should not be started acutely in HIT given early protein C depletion and skin necrosis risk, and protamine reverses heparin rather than addressing HIT itself.

options.label: A
options.text: Continue heparin at a reduced dose

options.label: B
options.text: Discontinue heparin and start argatroban

options.label: C
options.text: Discontinue heparin and start warfarin immediately

options.label: D
options.text: Administer protamine sulfate

stem: A patient is prescribed a high-potency topical corticosteroid for a resistant plaque of psoriasis on the elbow, for an extended course. Which of the following are recognized risks of prolonged use? Select all that apply.
rationale: Prolonged high-potency topical corticosteroid use carries real risk of skin atrophy, permanent striae, and — with sufficient potency, surface area, duration, or occlusion — systemic HPA axis suppression. Reversible hyperpigmentation and site-specific hair growth are not characteristic, well-established risks of this class.

options.label: A
options.text: Skin atrophy

options.label: B
options.text: Permanent striae

options.label: C
options.text: Hyperpigmentation reversible within days

options.label: D
options.text: Systemic HPA axis suppression with extensive use

options.label: E
options.text: Increased hair growth confined to the application site

stem: A 68-year-old man with open-angle glaucoma has been using timolol ophthalmic drops for 3 months. He returns to his pulmonologist for a routine COPD follow-up and reports new-onset wheezing and shortness of breath that began around the same time he started the eye drops, with a decline in FEV1 since his last visit. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
rationale: Topical ophthalmic beta-blockers like timolol can be absorbed systemically via nasolacrimal drainage in amounts sufficient to cause the same bronchoconstriction risk as an oral non-selective beta-blocker in a patient with underlying reactive airway disease.

options.label: A
options.text: Coincidental COPD progression unrelated to the eye drops

options.label: B
options.text: Systemic absorption of timolol via the nasolacrimal duct causing bronchoconstriction

options.label: C
options.text: An allergic reaction to the eye drop preservative

options.label: D
options.text: Progression of his glaucoma affecting respiratory centers

stem: Which of the following best describes the "Swiss cheese model" of medication error causation?
rationale: The Swiss cheese model conceptualizes layered system defenses, each with small inherent gaps; a serious error generally requires the gaps in multiple layers to align, reframing prevention as a systems-design problem rather than solely individual blame.

options.label: A
options.text: Errors occur exclusively due to individual carelessness

options.label: B
options.text: Serious errors typically require multiple system-layer defenses to fail simultaneously

options.label: C
options.text: Errors are prevented entirely by a single robust verification step

options.label: D
options.text: The model applies only to dispensing errors, not prescribing errors

stem: A 29-year-old woman with major depressive disorder has been taking phenelzine for the past 6 weeks with good symptom control. She calls the pharmacy asking whether she can start taking an over-the-counter cold medication containing pseudoephedrine for nasal congestion. What is the most appropriate response?
rationale: MAOIs like phenelzine broadly increase catecholamine availability; combining with a sympathomimetic decongestant risks a dangerous hypertensive crisis, an interaction distinct from and more serious than a simple timing-based concern.

options.label: A
options.text: Approve the request, as pseudoephedrine has no significant interaction with phenelzine

options.label: B
options.text: Advise against it, given the risk of a hypertensive crisis from the combined sympathomimetic and MAOI effect

options.label: C
options.text: Approve the request, but recommend taking the two medications 2 hours apart

options.label: D
options.text: Advise against it only because pseudoephedrine causes sedation

stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder and significant malnutrition is admitted to the hospital after several days without adequate oral intake. The medical team begins a full-calorie enteral feeding regimen on hospital day 1. On day 2, his phosphate has dropped from 3.2 mg/dL to 1.1 mg/dL, and he develops new atrial fibrillation. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
rationale: Refeeding syndrome occurs when nutritional support is reintroduced too aggressively in a severely malnourished patient; the resulting insulin surge drives phosphate (along with potassium and magnesium) intracellularly, causing a rapid drop in serum levels that can precipitate cardiac arrhythmias and other serious complications.

options.label: A
options.text: An unrelated cardiac arrhythmia coincidentally timed with feeding

options.label: B
options.text: Refeeding syndrome, from an insulin-mediated intracellular shift of phosphate triggered by aggressive nutritional reintroduction

options.label: C
options.text: A direct toxic effect of the enteral formula on cardiac tissue

options.label: D
options.text: Hypercalcemia from excessive calcium content in the formula

stem: A pharmacist is asked a complex question about comparative efficacy between two newer biologic agents for a specific, uncommon indication. Which type of resource is most likely to provide the most current, complete answer?
rationale: Tertiary resources are efficient for routine, well-established questions, but may lag behind current evidence for a comparative efficacy question involving newer agents and an uncommon indication — primary literature or a current systematic review provides the more complete, up-to-date answer here.

options.label: A
options.text: A standard tertiary drug compendium

options.label: B
options.text: Primary literature or a current systematic review

options.label: C
options.text: A patient package insert

options.label: D
options.text: A drug interaction database

stem: A 16-year-old girl with severe nodulocystic acne unresponsive to oral antibiotics and topical retinoids is started on isotretinoin. Four weeks into therapy, her mother calls the pharmacy concerned that her daughter has seemed unusually withdrawn and has made a comment about "not wanting to be here anymore." What is the most appropriate pharmacist response?
rationale: Isotretinoin therapy requires ongoing monitoring for mood and psychiatric symptom changes; a statement suggesting self-harm risk warrants prompt evaluation, not reassurance or dismissal, given the seriousness of what's being described.

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure the mother that mood changes are not associated with isotretinoin

options.label: B
options.text: Advise the mother to seek prompt evaluation, given isotretinoin's association with mood and psychiatric symptom changes requiring monitoring

options.label: C
options.text: Recommend simply reducing the isotretinoin dose without further evaluation

options.label: D
options.text: Advise that this is an expected, temporary side effect requiring no action

stem: A pharmacist reviews a prescription and identifies that a colleague dispensed the wrong strength of a medication to a patient two days earlier, though no adverse outcome has occurred. Which of the following best reflects the appropriate ethical approach to this situation?
rationale: The ethical obligation to disclose a medication error to the affected patient exists independently of the separate legal liability question, and is not contingent on whether harm has already manifested.

options.label: A
options.text: No action is needed since no harm occurred

options.label: B
options.text: The error should be disclosed to the patient, a step considered ethically distinct from any determination of legal liability

options.label: C
options.text: Disclosure should wait until it is confirmed the pharmacy has no legal liability

options.label: D
options.text: Only the colleague who made the error needs to be informed

stem: A clinical trial reports a relative risk reduction (RRR) of 40% for a new medication in preventing myocardial infarction. Which additional piece of information is necessary to determine the medication's actual clinical impact?
rationale: RRR alone doesn't convey the actual magnitude of benefit — the same RRR can represent a very different absolute benefit depending on the baseline event rate; absolute risk reduction (and the resulting NNT) requires knowing that baseline rate.

options.label: A
options.text: The p-value alone

options.label: B
options.text: The baseline (absolute) event rate in the control group

options.label: C
options.text: The total number of patients enrolled

options.label: D
options.text: The trial's funding source

stem: A nonsterile compounded oral suspension is prepared using ingredients for which specific stability data is unavailable for this exact formulation. Which of the following most accurately describes how the beyond-use date should generally be determined?
rationale: Absent specific stability data, USP <795> nonsterile compounding beyond-use dating defaults to the shorter of a defined maximum period or a percentage of the shortest remaining ingredient expiration — reflecting that compounded stability can't exceed that of its least stable component.

options.label: A
options.text: Always exactly one year from the date of compounding

options.label: B
options.text: The shorter of a defined maximum period or a percentage of the shortest remaining expiration date among the ingredients used

options.label: C
options.text: Indefinitely stable, since compounded products don't expire

options.label: D
options.text: Based solely on the expiration date of the active ingredient, ignoring other components

stem: A patient receiving enteral tube feeding is also prescribed phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis. The nursing staff administers the phenytoin suspension directly through the feeding tube without interrupting the feeds. Over the next several days, the patient experiences a breakthrough seizure despite an apparently appropriate phenytoin dose. What is the most likely explanation?
rationale: Enteral feeding formulas are well-documented to significantly reduce phenytoin absorption; feeds should be held for a period before and after phenytoin administration to allow adequate absorption, and failing to do so can result in subtherapeutic levels despite an appropriate ordered dose.

options.label: A
options.text: The phenytoin dose was calculated incorrectly

options.label: B
options.text: Enteral feeding formula significantly reduced phenytoin absorption

options.label: C
options.text: The patient developed a new drug allergy

options.label: D
options.text: Phenytoin is ineffective when administered via any route other than oral tablets

stem: A pharmacist compounding a sterile preparation determines it falls into a higher USP <797> risk category due to multiple manipulations performed in a less controlled environment. How should this most directly affect the beyond-use date assigned?
rationale: Higher-risk sterile preparations (more manipulations, less environmental control) carry increased contamination risk, and a correspondingly shorter beyond-use date directly reflects that risk under USP <797> risk-level stratification.

options.label: A
options.text: The beyond-use date should be longer to compensate for the higher risk

options.label: B
options.text: The beyond-use date should be shorter, reflecting the increased contamination risk

options.label: C
options.text: Risk category has no bearing on beyond-use dating

options.label: D
options.text: The preparation cannot be assigned any beyond-use date

stem: A 58-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m²) has routine labs showing calcium 8.4 mg/dL, phosphate 6.2 mg/dL, and an elevated intact PTH. Which of the following medication classes most directly addresses the elevated phosphate in this setting?
rationale: Phosphate binders (e.g., sevelamer, calcium acetate) reduce dietary phosphate absorption in the gut, directly addressing hyperphosphatemia that develops as GFR declines and drives the CKD-mineral bone disorder cascade, including secondary hyperparathyroidism.

options.label: A
options.text: Loop diuretics

options.label: B
options.text: Phosphate binders

options.label: C
options.text: ACE inhibitors

options.label: D
options.text: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents

stem: Which of the following best explains why protein C's short half-life contributes to an early hypercoagulable state when warfarin therapy is initiated without bridging anticoagulation?
rationale: Protein C is vitamin K-dependent like the procoagulant factors warfarin ultimately suppresses, but its shorter half-life means its anticoagulant activity drops faster than the procoagulant factors' activity early in therapy — creating a transient hypercoagulable window, the rationale behind bridging anticoagulation and the mechanism behind warfarin-induced skin necrosis risk.

options.label: A
options.text: Protein C has no relationship to warfarin's mechanism

options.label: B
options.text: Protein C, a natural anticoagulant, is also vitamin K-dependent and has a shorter half-life than several procoagulant clotting factors, so its levels fall faster early in therapy

options.label: C
options.text: Warfarin directly activates protein C

options.label: D
options.text: Protein C levels are unaffected by warfarin

stem: A 34-year-old woman with HIV has a CD4 count of 45 cells/mm³. She is already established on PCP prophylaxis. Which of the following is most appropriate to add given this specific CD4 count?
rationale: MAC (Mycobacterium avium complex) prophylaxis, typically with azithromycin or clarithromycin, is indicated once CD4 falls below approximately 50 cells/mm³ — layered on top of the already-indicated PCP prophylaxis that begins at CD4 under 200.

options.label: A
options.text: Azithromycin for MAC prophylaxis

options.label: B
options.text: Isoniazid for latent TB regardless of testing status

options.label: C
options.text: Oseltamivir for influenza prophylaxis

options.label: D
options.text: Acyclovir for herpes prophylaxis

stem: A patient with metastatic breast cancer receiving doxorubicin has had a cumulative lifetime dose approaching the recognized threshold associated with significantly increased risk of a specific organ toxicity. Which organ system is of greatest concern with continued use?
rationale: Anthracyclines like doxorubicin carry a well-recognized, cumulative-dose-dependent cardiotoxicity risk; monitoring LVEF/cardiac function and tracking cumulative lifetime dose are essential to minimize this risk as therapy continues.

options.label: A
options.text: Renal

options.label: B
options.text: Cardiac

options.label: C
options.text: Pulmonary

options.label: D
options.text: Hepatic

stem: A 52-year-old man with severe COPD (frequent exacerbations, elevated blood eosinophils on recent labs) is currently maintained on a LAMA-LABA combination inhaler. His pulmonologist wants to add a medication specifically to reduce exacerbation frequency given his eosinophil count. Which of the following is most appropriate?
rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids are selectively beneficial in COPD patients with frequent exacerbations and elevated eosinophil counts specifically, reducing exacerbation frequency in this subgroup — a more targeted addition than the other options, though ICS use in COPD does carry an increased pneumonia risk requiring consideration.

options.label: A
options.text: A short-acting beta agonist used more frequently

options.label: B
options.text: An inhaled corticosteroid

options.label: C
options.text: Roflumilast

options.label: D
options.text: A leukotriene receptor antagonist

stem: Which of the following beta-blockers has NOT been shown to reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and is therefore not the preferred choice for this specific indication?
rationale: Metoprolol tartrate (immediate-release) lacks the mortality-benefit evidence base in HFrEF that carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (extended-release), and bisoprolol have — an important distinction between immediate- and extended-release metoprolol formulations for this specific indication.

options.label: A
options.text: Carvedilol

options.label: B
options.text: Metoprolol succinate

options.label: C
options.text: Metoprolol tartrate

options.label: D
options.text: Bisoprolol

stem: A 68-year-old man weighs 80 kg and has a serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL. Using the Cockcroft-Gault equation, calculate his estimated creatinine clearance in mL/min. Round to the nearest whole number.
rationale: CrCl = [(140−age) × weight] / (72 × SCr) = [(140−68) × 80] / (72 × 1.2) = 5760 / 86.4 ≈ 67 mL/min. No female correction factor applies since the patient is male.

stem: A patient asks a pharmacist to recommend an OTC product for her 5-year-old child's persistent diarrhea, which has included visible blood in the stool over the past day. What is the most appropriate pharmacist response?
rationale: Bloody diarrhea suggests a possible infectious or inflammatory process where antimotility agents like loperamide are specifically inappropriate and could worsen the underlying process; this presentation exceeds appropriate OTC self-treatment and warrants referral.

options.label: A
options.text: Recommend loperamide dosed by weight

options.label: B
options.text: Recommend bismuth subsalicylate

options.label: C
options.text: Refer the child for prompt medical evaluation rather than recommending an OTC antidiarrheal

options.label: D
options.text: Recommend an oral rehydration solution alone with no further action needed

stem: A patient stabilized on long-term therapy with a specific manufacturer's phenytoin experiences a breakthrough seizure shortly after their pharmacy fills the prescription with a different manufacturer's generic version at pickup. Which category of drug does this scenario most directly illustrate the substitution risk for?
rationale: Phenytoin is a classic narrow therapeutic index drug; even AB-rated generic substitution carries a genuine, if often modest, risk of clinically meaningful level fluctuation for NTI drugs specifically, given the narrow margin between therapeutic and toxic/subtherapeutic concentration.

options.label: A
options.text: Any drug with an AB rating

options.label: B
options.text: Narrow therapeutic index drugs

options.label: C
options.text: Drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 specifically

options.label: D
options.text: Drugs requiring refrigeration

stem: Which of the following best exemplifies an "independent double-check" as a medication error prevention strategy?
rationale: An independent double-check specifically involves a second qualified person separately verifying a calculation or product, particularly emphasized for high-alert medications — providing a genuine additional layer of verification distinct from a single individual's self-check or reliance on technology alone.

options.label: A
options.text: A single pharmacist verifying their own calculation twice

options.label: B
options.text: A second qualified individual independently verifying a high-alert medication calculation or product before it reaches the patient

options.label: C
options.text: Relying solely on electronic health record alerts

options.label: D
options.text: A pharmacy technician performing all verification steps alone

stem: A patient asks a pharmacist to recommend an OTC product for a child's cough that is described as dry and disruptive to sleep, without significant mucus production. Which mechanism-matched option is most appropriate?
rationale: A dry, disruptive cough without significant mucus production is better matched to a cough suppressant like dextromethorphan, which acts centrally to reduce the cough reflex — distinct from guaifenesin, which is intended for a productive, mucus-heavy cough.

options.label: A
options.text: Guaifenesin, to thin mucus secretions

options.label: B
options.text: Dextromethorphan, to suppress the cough reflex

options.label: C
options.text: An antibiotic

options.label: D
options.text: A decongestant alone

stem: A patient with CKD stage 3 is started on an ACE inhibitor for proteinuria reduction. Which of the following are appropriate components of ongoing monitoring for this patient? Select all that apply.
rationale: ACE inhibitors require monitoring for hyperkalemia (via reduced aldosterone activity) and changes in renal function (a modest expected SCr rise is common, but significant increases require evaluation), alongside blood pressure response to therapy. LFTs and CBC are not core, specific monitoring parameters for ACE inhibitor therapy itself.

options.label: A
options.text: Serum potassium

options.label: B
options.text: Serum creatinine/renal function

options.label: C
options.text: Liver function tests

options.label: D
options.text: Blood pressure

options.label: E
options.text: Complete blood count

stem: A 3-year-old child is brought to urgent care with a fever and is found to have chickenpox. The parent asks whether they can give the child a fever reducer they have at home containing aspirin. What is the most appropriate pharmacist counseling point?
rationale: Aspirin use in children with a viral illness — classically chickenpox or influenza — carries Reye syndrome risk; acetaminophen or ibuprofen are the standard, preferred antipyretic options in this population.

options.label: A
options.text: Aspirin is appropriate and preferred for viral illness in children

options.label: B
options.text: Aspirin should be avoided given the association with Reye syndrome in children with viral illness

options.label: C
options.text: Aspirin should only be avoided if the child is under 1 year of age

options.label: D
options.text: Aspirin is safe as long as the dose is halved

stem: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her family for new-onset confusion that developed over the past day. She has a known history of mild dementia, but her baseline cognitive function has been stable for the past year. Her family notes she was started on a new medication for overactive bladder about a week ago. Which of the following is most likely contributing to her acute presentation?
rationale: An acute change from a stable cognitive baseline — especially temporally linked to a new anticholinergic medication (a common OAB treatment class) — should prompt recognition of delirium superimposed on dementia, with the new medication as a specific, reversible contributing factor to investigate, rather than assuming the change simply reflects dementia progression.

options.label: A
options.text: Progression of her underlying dementia

options.label: B
options.text: An anticholinergic medication precipitating delirium

options.label: C
options.text: Normal age-related cognitive decline

options.label: D
options.text: An unrelated psychiatric condition

stem: A pharmacist is asked by a patient's adult child to share details about the patient's current medications and health conditions without the patient's knowledge or consent, citing concern for the patient's wellbeing. What is the most appropriate response, assuming no legal authorization such as a healthcare proxy has been established?
rationale: Patient confidentiality permits disclosure for treatment, payment, and healthcare operations purposes, or specific legally mandated reporting — a family member's request without patient consent or documented legal authorization does not fall under a permitted exception.

options.label: A
options.text: Share the information, since the request comes from a family member

options.label: B
options.text: Decline to share the information, as unauthorized disclosure outside the treatment/payment/operations framework is not appropriate absent patient consent or legal authorization

options.label: C
options.text: Share only the medication names but not the associated conditions

options.label: D
options.text: Share the information but ask the family member to keep it confidential

stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy develops a fever with an absolute neutrophil count of 400 cells/mm³. What is the most appropriate immediate management approach?
rationale: Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency requiring immediate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (typically with antipseudomonal coverage) given the risk of rapid clinical deterioration in a patient with significantly impaired immune defense.

options.label: A
options.text: Outpatient observation without antibiotics

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, given the risk of rapid deterioration in febrile neutropenia

options.label: C
options.text: Waiting for culture results before starting any treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Antipyretics alone are sufficient

stem: A pharmacist is evaluating a research study to inform a clinical decision and notes that participants were randomly assigned to treatment or control groups. What is the primary methodological benefit of randomization in this context?
rationale: Randomization's core methodological benefit is balancing confounding variables — both those researchers thought to measure and those they didn't — across groups, supporting more confident attribution of an observed outcome difference to the intervention itself.

options.label: A
options.text: It guarantees the study will reach statistical significance

options.label: B
options.text: It distributes both known and unknown confounding variables roughly evenly between groups

options.label: C
options.text: It eliminates the need for a control group

options.label: D
options.text: It ensures the study can be conducted without informed consent

stem: A patient with a documented sulfa allergy requires a diuretic for volume management. Which of the following best reflects the appropriate consideration given a structural relationship to sulfonamide antibiotics?
rationale: Furosemide and thiazide diuretics do contain a sulfonamide-related chemical structure, prompting historical caution in sulfa-allergic patients — though true clinically significant cross-reactivity is often more nuanced and less absolute than a blanket avoidance approach would suggest, warranting informed clinical judgment rather than automatic exclusion.

options.label: A
options.text: This is a non-issue; thiazide diuretics have no structural relationship to sulfonamide antibiotics

options.label: B
options.text: Furosemide and thiazide diuretics both contain a sulfonamide moiety, though true cross-reactivity concerns are often more nuanced than a blanket avoidance rule suggests

options.label: C
options.text: All diuretics must be avoided in any patient with any drug allergy

options.label: D
options.text: Only potassium-sparing diuretics are safe in sulfa-allergic patients

stem: Which of the following is an appropriate practice when initiating nutritional support in a patient identified as high-risk for refeeding syndrome?
rationale: In a patient identified as high-risk for refeeding syndrome, cautious initiation with lower caloric intake, gradual advancement, and proactive electrolyte monitoring is the appropriate preventive approach, given the danger of an abrupt, large insulin-mediated electrolyte shift with aggressive refeeding.

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately providing full estimated caloric needs

options.label: B
options.text: Starting with a lower caloric intake and advancing gradually while closely monitoring phosphate, potassium, and magnesium

options.label: C
options.text: Withholding all electrolyte supplementation until symptoms develop

options.label: D
options.text: Refeeding syndrome risk has no bearing on how nutritional support should be initiated

stem: A meta-analysis pools results from 15 individual randomized controlled trials addressing the same clinical question. Which of the following most directly affects the reliability of this meta-analysis's conclusions?
rationale: A meta-analysis's reliability is contingent on the quality and consistency of the individual studies it pools — combining a large number of low-quality or highly inconsistent studies does not automatically produce a more trustworthy conclusion than a single well-designed study.

options.label: A
options.text: The total number of studies alone, regardless of quality

options.label: B
options.text: The quality and consistency of the individual studies being pooled

options.label: C
options.text: Meta-analyses are always reliable regardless of what they include

options.label: D
options.text: Only the most recent study in the pool matters

stem: An 80-year-old woman weighs 50 kg and has a serum creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL, which appears "normal" on her lab report. Using the Cockcroft-Gault equation, calculate her estimated creatinine clearance in mL/min. Round to the nearest whole number.
rationale: CrCl = [(140−80) × 50] / (72 × 0.9) × 0.85 ≈ 39 mL/min. Despite an apparently "normal" serum creatinine, her calculated CrCl is significantly reduced — illustrating why relying on creatinine alone in older adults with reduced muscle mass can substantially underestimate true renal impairment.

stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia has been treatment-resistant to two adequate trials of different atypical antipsychotics. His psychiatrist wants to initiate a medication specifically indicated for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Which of the following requires mandatory, ongoing hematologic monitoring due to a risk of severe neutropenia?
rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia given its agranulocytosis/severe neutropenia risk, requiring mandatory, scheduled absolute neutrophil count monitoring throughout therapy — a distinguishing safety requirement not shared by the other listed atypical antipsychotics.

options.label: A
options.text: Risperidone

options.label: B
options.text: Aripiprazole

options.label: C
options.text: Clozapine

options.label: D
options.text: Quetiapine

stem: A patient is prescribed both extended-release oxycodone and immediate-release hydrocodone-acetaminophen from two different prescribers without either being aware of the other prescription. Which category of drug utilization review would most likely catch this scenario?
rationale: Concurrent opioid prescriptions from different prescribers, unaware of each other, represents a therapeutic duplication concern — DUR systems are specifically designed to flag this kind of overlap across a patient's full medication profile.

options.label: A
options.text: Age-appropriateness screening

options.label: B
options.text: Therapeutic duplication

options.label: C
options.text: Dose/duration screening only

options.label: D
options.text: This scenario would not be flagged by any DUR category

stem: A pharmacist wants to determine the appropriate route of administration and typical dosing range for a well-established medication being used for a routine, common indication. Which resource type is most efficient for this need?
rationale: For routine, well-established dosing and administration questions, a tertiary reference provides efficient, appropriately reliable information — reserving primary literature consultation for more novel or contested clinical questions.

options.label: A
options.text: A primary research article

options.label: B
options.text: A standard tertiary drug reference

options.label: C
options.text: An unpublished case report

options.label: D
options.text: A conference abstract

stem: A 20-year-old man with severe nodulocystic acne is being started on isotretinoin. He asks the pharmacist why he needs monthly blood tests during treatment. Which of the following is an appropriate explanation for this monitoring?
rationale: Isotretinoin requires ongoing monitoring beyond pregnancy testing alone, including liver function tests, lipid panels (given hypertriglyceridemia risk), and mood/psychiatric symptom screening throughout therapy.

options.label: A
options.text: Monitoring is not actually necessary and is done only for legal reasons

options.label: B
options.text: Isotretinoin requires monitoring for hepatotoxicity, hypertriglyceridemia, and mood/psychiatric changes throughout therapy

options.label: C
options.text: Blood tests are only needed once, at the start of treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Monitoring is solely for pregnancy testing

stem: A patient with a history of gout is switched from allopurinol to febuxostat due to inadequate response. Which of the following is an important consideration with this switch?
rationale: Febuxostat, like allopurinol, is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, but comparative trial data has raised a cardiovascular death signal with febuxostat specifically — making it generally reserved as a second-line option for patients who fail or cannot tolerate allopurinol.

options.label: A
options.text: Febuxostat has no cardiovascular risk considerations

options.label: B
options.text: Febuxostat is an alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor, but comparative trial data has noted a cardiovascular death signal, making it generally reserved for patients who fail or cannot tolerate allopurinol

options.label: C
options.text: Febuxostat works through a completely different, unrelated mechanism from allopurinol

options.label: D
options.text: Febuxostat requires no monitoring of any kind

stem: An 84-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment is prescribed diphenhydramine for seasonal allergy symptoms by an urgent care provider unfamiliar with his full medical history. Which of the following is the most significant concern with this choice in this specific patient?
rationale: First-generation antihistamines like diphenhydramine cross the blood-brain barrier and carry significant anticholinergic burden, a specific Beers Criteria concern in older adults given increased fall risk, confusion, and — with cumulative anticholinergic exposure — long-term cognitive decline risk, particularly relevant in a patient with existing mild cognitive impairment.

options.label: A
options.text: Diphenhydramine is ineffective for allergy symptoms

options.label: B
options.text: First-generation antihistamines carry meaningful anticholinergic burden and cognitive risk in older adults

options.label: C
options.text: Diphenhydramine requires renal dose adjustment that was likely overlooked

options.label: D
options.text: Diphenhydramine has no significant interaction concerns in elderly patients

stem: A patient with acute leukemia undergoing induction chemotherapy develops rapidly rising potassium, phosphate, and uric acid levels with declining calcium 48 hours after treatment initiation. Which of the following best describes this presentation?
rationale: Tumor lysis syndrome results from massive, rapid malignant cell death releasing intracellular potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, with the resulting hyperphosphatemia binding calcium and driving hypocalcemia — a recognized, potentially serious complication of chemotherapy in high-tumor-burden malignancies, requiring prophylaxis/management with agents like allopurinol or rasburicase.

options.label: A
options.text: Chemotherapy-induced renal failure unrelated to tumor burden

options.label: B
options.text: Tumor lysis syndrome, from the rapid release of intracellular contents as malignant cells die

options.label: C
options.text: An unrelated electrolyte disturbance from IV fluids

options.label: D
options.text: Expected, clinically insignificant laboratory fluctuation

stem: A 62-year-old man with BPH has been taking tamsulosin for 8 months with good symptom control. He is scheduled for cataract surgery next month. Which of the following is the most important counseling point regarding his tamsulosin use?
rationale: Tamsulosin's alpha-1 blockade can cause Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome during cataract surgery; this risk persists even if the drug is stopped before surgery, since the iris changes may not fully reverse — disclosure to the surgical team, regardless of current use status, allows the surgeon to adjust technique proactively.

options.label: A
options.text: He should stop tamsulosin permanently before any future eye procedures

options.label: B
options.text: His use of tamsulosin, even if discontinued before surgery, should be disclosed to his ophthalmologist given the risk of Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome

options.label: C
options.text: Tamsulosin has no relevance to eye surgery and does not need to be mentioned

options.label: D
options.text: He should double his tamsulosin dose before surgery to reduce urinary symptoms during recovery

stem: A patient using a topical prostaglandin analog for open-angle glaucoma asks the pharmacist about a cosmetic change she has noticed since starting therapy. Which of the following is a recognized effect of this drug class?
rationale: Prostaglandin analogs like latanoprost are associated with increased iris pigmentation (which can be permanent, particularly in mixed-color irises) and increased eyelash length/growth — recognized, visible cosmetic effects worth proactive patient counseling.

options.label: A
options.text: Permanent vision loss

options.label: B
options.text: Increased iris pigmentation and eyelash growth

options.label: C
options.text: Complete loss of eyelashes

options.label: D
options.text: Skin depigmentation around the eyes

stem: A pharmacist is evaluating a study and notes that participants and outcome assessors were both unaware of group assignment throughout the study. This design feature is best described as which of the following?
rationale: Double-blinding refers to both participants and outcome assessors being unaware of group assignment, reducing the risk that expectation or bias from either party influences reported or assessed outcomes — distinct from randomization, which addresses confounding through balanced group assignment.

options.label: A
options.text: Randomization

options.label: B
options.text: Double-blinding

options.label: C
options.text: Stratification

options.label: D
options.text: Crossover design

stem: A 45-year-old man taking sildenafil as needed for erectile dysfunction is prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin after a new diagnosis of stable angina. He asks the pharmacist if it's safe to take both medications as prescribed, using proper timing. What is the most appropriate response?
rationale: The interaction between PDE5 inhibitors and nitrates is an absolute contraindication, given convergent nitric oxide/cGMP pathway effects risking profound, dangerous hypotension — this cannot be safely managed through timing separation or dose adjustment, and the prescriber should be contacted to select an alternative approach.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, as long as at least 2 hours separate the two medications

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, but only using the lowest sildenafil dose

options.label: C
options.text: No, combining a PDE5 inhibitor with any nitrate is an absolute contraindication regardless of timing

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, this combination has no significant interaction

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is HIV-negative wants to start pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to reduce her risk of HIV acquisition. Which of the following must be confirmed before initiating oral PrEP?
rationale: Confirming HIV-negative status before starting PrEP is essential, since starting the NRTI-based regimen in a patient with undiagnosed HIV infection risks developing viral resistance to these same medications, which are also core components of HIV treatment regimens.

options.label: A
options.text: A recent normal complete blood count

options.label: B
options.text: Confirmed HIV-negative status via testing

options.label: C
options.text: A normal chest X-ray

options.label: D
options.text: Confirmed hepatitis C status only

stem: A patient declines a pharmacist's recommendation to start a statin for primary cardiovascular prevention despite understanding the potential benefit, citing personal preference. Which ethical principle most directly supports respecting this decision?
rationale: Autonomy is the principle protecting a patient's right to make their own informed healthcare decisions, including declining a recommended, beneficial therapy — the appropriate response is ensuring the patient is adequately informed, not overriding an autonomous, informed choice.

options.label: A
options.text: Justice

options.label: B
options.text: Autonomy

options.label: C
options.text: Nonmaleficence

options.label: D
options.text: Confidentiality

stem: A 32-year-old woman with severe cystic acne has failed treatment with oral antibiotics and topical retinoids. Her dermatologist wants to start isotretinoin. Which of the following is a required component of dispensing this medication under its risk management program?
rationale: Isotretinoin's REMS-based pregnancy prevention program requires documented negative pregnancy testing and structured enrollment confirmation before dispensing, a mandatory example of Elements to Assure Safe Use (ETASU) given the drug's severe teratogenic risk.

options.label: A
options.text: A signed liability waiver

options.label: B
options.text: Documented negative pregnancy test and program enrollment confirmation

options.label: C
options.text: A note from an unrelated specialist

options.label: D
options.text: Verbal confirmation only, without documentation

stem: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites is treated with a combination of spironolactone and furosemide. What is the primary rationale for using these two diuretics together in this setting?
rationale: Cirrhotic ascites is substantially driven by RAAS activation and resulting sodium retention; spironolactone directly addresses this mechanism, while furosemide adds complementary diuretic effect — the combination is standard, mechanism-based management for cirrhotic ascites, not primarily about maximizing diuresis indiscriminately.

options.label: A
options.text: To maximize diuresis regardless of mechanism

options.label: B
options.text: Spironolactone addresses the underlying RAAS-driven sodium retention characteristic of cirrhotic ascites, while furosemide adds additional diuretic effect

options.label: C
options.text: Furosemide is required to counteract spironolactone's hypertensive effect

options.label: D
options.text: The combination prevents hepatic encephalopathy

stem: A pharmacy receives a new prescription for a Schedule II controlled substance with three refills written on it. What is the most appropriate action?
rationale: Schedule II substances permit no refills on a single prescription under federal law; a new prescription is required for additional quantity, making this refill notation inconsistent with federal requirements and warranting prescriber contact.

options.label: A
options.text: Fill the prescription and all three refills as written

options.label: B
options.text: Contact the prescriber, since Schedule II prescriptions do not permit refills under federal law

options.label: C
options.text: Fill only one refill and disregard the rest

options.label: D
options.text: Fill the refills only if the patient requests them within 30 days

stem: A patient is to receive an IV infusion at a rate of 5 mcg/kg/min. The patient weighs 70 kg, and the infusion bag contains 250 mg of drug in 250 mL of fluid (concentration 1000 mcg/mL). What infusion rate should be programmed on the pump, in mL/hr? Round to the nearest whole number.
rationale: 5 mcg/kg/min × 70 kg = 350 mcg/min × 60 min/hr = 21,000 mcg/hr. Dividing by the concentration (1000 mcg/mL) gives 21 mL/hr.

stem: A compounding pharmacist needs to prepare 480 mL of a 2.5% w/v solution using a stock 10% w/v solution and an appropriate diluent. How many mL of the 10% stock solution are needed? Round to the nearest whole number.
rationale: Using C1V1 = C2V2: (10%)(V1) = (2.5%)(480 mL), so V1 = (2.5 × 480) / 10 = 120 mL of the 10% stock solution needed, with the remaining volume made up with diluent.

stem: A pharmacist is verifying a prescription for an oral suspension requiring reconstitution. Which of the following pieces of information is essential before calculating the correct amount of diluent water to add?
rationale: Reconstitution calculations require knowing the target final concentration and total finished volume to determine the correct diluent volume to add — information directly tied to the calculation itself, unlike the other listed options.

options.label: A
options.text: The patient's insurance information

options.label: B
options.text: The final concentration desired and the total volume the finished product should yield

options.label: C
options.text: The color of the bottle

options.label: D
options.text: The prescribing physician's specialty

stem: A patient asks a pharmacist to recommend a decongestant for nasal congestion. The patient mentions a history of poorly controlled hypertension. What is the most appropriate counseling point?
rationale: Decongestants like pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine cause vasoconstriction via sympathomimetic activity, which can raise blood pressure — a specific caution in patients with poorly controlled hypertension, warranting either an alternative recommendation or physician input rather than routine, unconditional use.

options.label: A
options.text: Recommend pseudoephedrine at the standard dose with no additional caution

options.label: B
options.text: Advise caution given decongestants' vasoconstrictive/sympathomimetic effect, which can raise blood pressure, and consider an alternative or physician consultation

options.label: C
options.text: Recommend doubling the dose for faster relief

options.label: D
options.text: Decongestants have no relevant interaction with blood pressure

stem: A pharmacist is preparing a hazardous sterile injectable chemotherapy product. Which type of primary engineering control is most appropriate for this preparation?
rationale: Biological safety cabinets provide dual protection — maintaining product sterility while also protecting compounding personnel from hazardous drug exposure — making them the appropriate choice for hazardous sterile preparations, unlike a standard laminar airflow workbench, which protects the product but not the compounder.

options.label: A
options.text: A standard laminar airflow workbench

options.label: B
options.text: A biological safety cabinet

options.label: C
options.text: No primary engineering control is required for sterile products

options.label: D
options.text: A standard fume hood used for nonsterile compounding

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe flank pain and is found to have a kidney stone on imaging. His urine pH is notably acidic, and stone analysis later confirms a uric acid stone. Which of the following is most appropriate for long-term prevention of recurrence?
rationale: Uric acid stones form specifically in acidic urine; potassium citrate alkalinizes the urine, directly addressing the chemistry driving this specific stone type — thiazides are more specifically useful for calcium stone prevention, and dietary calcium restriction can paradoxically worsen oxalate stone risk (a different stone type than described here).

options.label: A
options.text: Increased dietary calcium restriction

options.label: B
options.text: Potassium citrate to alkalinize the urine

options.label: C
options.text: A thiazide diuretic

options.label: D
options.text: Increased dietary oxalate intake

stem: A patient with a history of tendon rupture on a fluoroquinolone in the past requires antibiotic therapy for a new infection. Which of the following classes shares a boxed warning for tendon-related adverse effects with fluoroquinolones?
rationale: The tendinitis/tendon rupture boxed warning is specific to fluoroquinolones among commonly used antibiotic classes; macrolides, tetracyclines, and penicillins do not carry this same specific warning, making fluoroquinolone avoidance in this patient a class-specific decision rather than one requiring broader antibiotic avoidance.

options.label: A
options.text: Macrolides

options.label: B
options.text: None of the other major antibiotic classes carry this specific boxed warning

options.label: C
options.text: Tetracyclines

options.label: D
options.text: Penicillins

stem: A patient with a suspected herpetic corneal infection is prescribed a topical corticosteroid by an urgent care provider unfamiliar with the diagnosis, for presumed eye inflammation. What is the most important pharmacist intervention in this scenario?
rationale: Topical corticosteroids are specifically contraindicated in herpetic keratitis, since they can worsen HSV replication and disease progression — an important, easily-missed exception to the general instinct to reach for a corticosteroid for eye inflammation, requiring pharmacist intervention before dispensing.

options.label: A
options.text: Dispense as written with routine counseling

options.label: B
options.text: Contact the prescriber, since topical corticosteroids can worsen herpetic keratitis by promoting HSV replication

options.label: C
options.text: Recommend increasing the corticosteroid dose for faster symptom relief

options.label: D
options.text: No intervention needed since corticosteroids are generally safe for eye inflammation

stem: A patient with gout is prescribed colchicine for an acute flare. The patient's medication list also includes clarithromycin, recently started for a sinus infection. What is the most significant concern with this combination?
rationale: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitor, and colchicine is a substrate of both pathways — this combination carries a well-documented, potentially severe/fatal colchicine toxicity risk, making concurrent use a significant safety concern requiring alternative antibiotic selection or colchicine avoidance.

options.label: A
options.text: No significant interaction exists between these two medications

options.label: B
options.text: Clarithromycin's strong CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein inhibition can significantly increase colchicine levels, risking severe toxicity

options.label: C
options.text: Colchicine reduces the effectiveness of clarithromycin

options.label: D
options.text: The combination increases risk of hyperuricemia

stem: A pediatric patient requires an emergency medication dose, but their actual body weight is unknown and cannot be immediately measured. Which of the following tools is most appropriate for rapidly estimating an appropriate weight-based dose?
rationale: A length-based resuscitation tape provides a rapid, reasonably reliable weight estimate based on measured length when an actual weight is unavailable, allowing weight-based emergency dosing to proceed without the dangerous delay of waiting for an actual weight measurement.

options.label: A
options.text: Adult fixed-dose protocols

options.label: B
options.text: A length-based resuscitation tape

options.label: C
options.text: Estimating weight based on the child's stated age alone

options.label: D
options.text: Delaying treatment until an actual weight can be obtained

stem: A transplant recipient on tacrolimus develops a fungal infection requiring treatment with an azole antifungal. Which of the following is the most important consideration when initiating this combination?
rationale: Azole antifungals are potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, and tacrolimus is significantly metabolized by this pathway — starting an azole requires anticipatory tacrolimus dose reduction with follow-up trough level monitoring, rather than waiting to react only after an abnormal level or toxicity symptoms appear.

options.label: A
options.text: No dose adjustment of tacrolimus is needed

options.label: B
options.text: Azole antifungals inhibit CYP3A4, likely increasing tacrolimus levels and requiring anticipatory dose adjustment with follow-up monitoring

options.label: C
options.text: Tacrolimus should be permanently discontinued during antifungal therapy

options.label: D
options.text: The interaction only matters if the patient develops symptoms of toxicity

stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes presents in diabetic ketoacidosis with an initial potassium level of 3.0 mEq/L. The medical team plans to start an insulin infusion. What is the most appropriate immediate action regarding potassium?
rationale: Insulin drives potassium intracellularly; starting an insulin infusion in a patient with potassium already at 3.0 mEq/L risks precipitating dangerous hypokalemia — the correct sequence addresses fluids and potassium before or alongside insulin initiation, not insulin first in isolation.

options.label: A
options.text: Start insulin immediately; potassium can be addressed afterward

options.label: B
options.text: Begin potassium replacement before or concurrent with starting the insulin infusion

options.label: C
options.text: Withhold insulin indefinitely until potassium normalizes

options.label: D
options.text: Potassium replacement is not necessary in DKA management

stem: A pharmacist needs to quickly verify the standard adult dose of a well-established, commonly used medication for a routine prescription. Which type of resource is most appropriate for this specific need?
rationale: For routine, well-established dosing questions, a tertiary reference provides efficient, appropriately reliable information — reserving primary literature or systematic review consultation for more novel, contested, or highly specific clinical questions where tertiary sources may not be sufficient.

options.label: A
options.text: A primary research article

options.label: B
options.text: A standard tertiary drug reference

options.label: C
options.text: A systematic review

options.label: D
options.text: An unpublished conference abstract

stem: A pharmacy is preparing to dispense a medication that requires refrigerated storage. Upon receiving the shipment, the pharmacist notices the cold-chain temperature indicator shows the product was exposed to temperatures outside the appropriate range during transit, though the product appears visually unchanged. What is the most appropriate action?
rationale: A cold-chain failure can compromise a temperature-sensitive product's integrity and potency even without any visible change in appearance — visual inspection alone is not sufficient to confirm a product remains appropriately stable after a documented storage excursion, and such product should not be dispensed.

options.label: A
options.text: Dispense the product as normal since it appears visually unchanged

options.label: B
options.text: Do not dispense the product, since a cold-chain failure can compromise product integrity even without any visible change

options.label: C
options.text: Dispense the product but counsel the patient to store it at room temperature going forward

options.label: D
options.text: Refrigerate the product for an extended period before dispensing to "correct" the issue

stem: A patient with a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin requires antibiotic therapy for a serious infection. The infectious disease physician wants to use a cephalosporin. What is the most accurate counseling point regarding this decision?
rationale: Penicillin-cephalosporin cross-reactivity is now understood to be lower than historically assumed and substantially side-chain dependent rather than a uniform class effect, supporting individualized risk assessment rather than automatic avoidance of all cephalosporins in a penicillin-allergic patient.

options.label: A
options.text: Cephalosporins must always be avoided in any patient with a penicillin allergy

options.label: B
options.text: Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is lower than historically believed and is largely side-chain dependent, so a careful risk assessment is appropriate rather than blanket avoidance

options.label: C
options.text: Cephalosporins are chemically unrelated to penicillins and carry no cross-reactivity risk at all

options.label: D
options.text: Only oral cephalosporins carry cross-reactivity risk, not IV formulations

stem: A patient stabilized on warfarin therapy begins receiving enteral tube feeding after a stroke. Several days later, the patient's INR is found to be subtherapeutic despite no change in warfarin dose. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
rationale: Many enteral formulas contain vitamin K, which can directly antagonize warfarin's vitamin K-dependent clotting factor suppression — a patient starting enteral feeds while on warfarin may show unexpected INR changes traceable to this interaction.

options.label: A
options.text: The patient developed resistance to warfarin

options.label: B
options.text: The enteral formula contains vitamin K, which can antagonize warfarin's anticoagulant effect

options.label: C
options.text: Enteral feeding has no relevant interaction with warfarin

options.label: D
options.text: The INR result is a laboratory error

stem: A patient asks a pharmacist which OTC pain reliever is safest for occasional use given a documented allergy to aspirin causing urticaria. Which of the following requires the most caution given cross-reactivity concerns?
rationale: NSAIDs like ibuprofen share the same COX-inhibition mechanism as aspirin, and patients with aspirin-induced urticaria/reactions may experience similar reactions with other NSAIDs; acetaminophen, which works through a different mechanism, is generally the safer alternative in this scenario.

options.label: A
options.text: Acetaminophen

options.label: B
options.text: Ibuprofen, given shared COX-inhibition mechanism with aspirin

options.label: C
options.text: Topical hydrocortisone

options.label: D
options.text: Loratadine

stem: A hospitalized patient is receiving total parenteral nutrition. The pharmacist notes the current formulation provides dextrose as the primary calorie source. Approximately how many kilocalories does each gram of dextrose in the TPN solution provide?
rationale: Dextrose provides approximately 3.4 kcal/g in TPN solutions, distinct from protein/amino acids (4 kcal/g) and lipid emulsions (approximately 10 kcal/g, varying by product) — an important distinction for accurate TPN calorie calculations.

options.label: A
options.text: 4 kcal/g

options.label: B
options.text: 3.4 kcal/g

options.label: C
options.text: 9 kcal/g

options.label: D
options.text: 7 kcal/g

stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is started on methotrexate. Which of the following is routinely co-prescribed to reduce methotrexate-related toxicity?
rationale: Folic acid is routinely co-prescribed with methotrexate in RA management to reduce toxicity (particularly GI and hepatic effects) associated with methotrexate's folate-antagonist mechanism, without significantly compromising its immunomodulatory efficacy at RA doses.

options.label: A
options.text: Vitamin B12

options.label: B
options.text: Folic acid

options.label: C
options.text: Vitamin D

options.label: D
options.text: Iron supplementation

stem: A pharmacist wants to locate the original research study behind a claim made in a tertiary drug reference. Which resource type would most directly lead to this original source?
rationale: Secondary resources (such as bibliographic/indexing databases) are specifically designed to help locate primary literature — the actual original research studies — rather than serving as a substitute for reading and evaluating that primary source directly.

options.label: A
options.text: Another tertiary reference

options.label: B
options.text: A secondary bibliographic database used to search for primary literature

options.label: C
options.text: The product's package insert only

options.label: D
options.text: A drug interaction checker

stem: A pharmacist notices that a patient's medication list includes a new prescription for a proton pump inhibitor started shortly after the patient began taking an NSAID for chronic pain. Which phenomenon does this scenario most likely represent?
rationale: This pattern is consistent with a prescribing cascade — treating an NSAID's GI-irritant side effect with a PPI rather than reconsidering the NSAID itself — worth flagging for review to determine whether addressing the original drug is more appropriate than layering on additional therapy.

options.label: A
options.text: An unrelated coincidence

options.label: B
options.text: A prescribing cascade, where a drug's side effect was treated with an additional drug rather than addressing the original cause

options.label: C
options.text: Appropriate combination therapy with no further consideration needed

options.label: D
options.text: A medication error requiring disciplinary action

stem: Which of the following electrolytes has a valence of 2, requiring this value to be used when converting a mass-based dose to mEq?
rationale: Calcium and magnesium are divalent (valence 2), while sodium, potassium, and chloride are monovalent (valence 1) — an important distinction for accurate mEq calculations, since mEq = (mg × valence) / molecular weight.

options.label: A
options.text: Sodium

options.label: B
options.text: Potassium

options.label: C
options.text: Calcium

options.label: D
options.text: Chloride

stem: A 24-year-old woman with asthma reports using her albuterol inhaler nearly every day for symptom relief over the past month, in addition to her prescribed inhaled corticosteroid. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
rationale: Frequent short-acting beta agonist use is a recognized marker of poor asthma control, warranting reassessment of the treatment regimen (adherence, inhaler technique, or step-up therapy) rather than being accepted as a stable, well-controlled pattern.

options.label: A
options.text: Excellent asthma control requiring no changes

options.label: B
options.text: Poor asthma control, since frequent SABA use is a marker of inadequate control requiring reassessment

options.label: C
options.text: The albuterol inhaler is defective

options.label: D
options.text: The inhaled corticosteroid should be discontinued

stem: A patient asks for a recommendation for occasional heartburn that occurs about once a week after certain meals. Which of the following is a reasonable first-line OTC option?
rationale: For infrequent, mild heartburn, antacids or H2 receptor antagonists used as needed are appropriate first-line OTC options; OTC PPIs are generally labeled for a defined short course for more frequent symptoms, not indefinite daily use, and this presentation doesn't yet warrant referral.

options.label: A
options.text: An OTC-strength proton pump inhibitor for daily indefinite use

options.label: B
options.text: An antacid or H2 receptor antagonist for as-needed use

options.label: C
options.text: Referral is required for any heartburn symptoms

options.label: D
options.text: A prescription-strength PPI

stem: A patient with hypothyroidism has been stable on levothyroxine for years. She recently started a calcium supplement for bone health, taken at the same time each morning as her levothyroxine dose. At her next visit, her TSH is found to be elevated compared to her prior stable baseline. What is the most likely explanation?
rationale: Calcium (like iron and certain other agents) can bind levothyroxine in the gut and reduce its absorption; these should be separated in administration timing, and taking them together likely explains her reduced levothyroxine effect and resulting TSH elevation.

options.label: A
options.text: Her hypothyroidism has spontaneously worsened

options.label: B
options.text: Calcium can bind levothyroxine in the gut and reduce its absorption when taken together

options.label: C
options.text: The calcium supplement has no interaction with levothyroxine

options.label: D
options.text: Her levothyroxine dose was decreased in error

stem: A patient hospitalized with sepsis has blood cultures pending. The medical team wants to start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. Which of the following best describes the appropriate timing of antibiotic administration relative to obtaining cultures?
rationale: The sepsis hour-1 bundle emphasizes obtaining cultures before antibiotic administration when feasible (to preserve culture accuracy), but critically, antibiotic administration should never be delayed for this purpose given the significant mortality risk of delayed treatment in sepsis.

options.label: A
options.text: Antibiotics should be delayed until culture results return, to avoid affecting culture accuracy

options.label: B
options.text: Cultures should be obtained before antibiotics when possible, but antibiotic administration should not be delayed for this purpose

options.label: C
options.text: Cultures are not necessary if antibiotics are being started empirically

options.label: D
options.text: Antibiotics and cultures have no specific timing relationship

stem: A patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma presents to the emergency department with severe eye pain, redness, and blurred vision. Which of the following is part of the appropriate acute management approach?
rationale: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency; oral or IV acetazolamide is used to rapidly reduce intraocular pressure, alongside topical agents, as a bridge to definitive treatment with laser iridotomy — this presentation requires urgent, not delayed or outpatient, management.

options.label: A
options.text: Oral or IV acetazolamide to rapidly lower intraocular pressure

options.label: B
options.text: Reassurance and outpatient follow-up in one week

options.label: C
options.text: A prostaglandin analog as first-line acute therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Observation only, since angle-closure glaucoma resolves spontaneously

stem: A pediatrician wants to prescribe an oral pain reliever following a tonsillectomy for a 9-year-old child. Which of the following should be specifically avoided given a serious, potentially fatal risk in this context?
rationale: Codeine is contraindicated in children under 12, particularly flagged following tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy, given the risk of unpredictable, potentially fatal respiratory depression in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolizers who convert an unusually large proportion of codeine to its active opioid metabolite.

options.label: A
options.text: Acetaminophen

options.label: B
options.text: Ibuprofen

options.label: C
options.text: Codeine

options.label: D
options.text: A topical throat spray

stem: A pharmacist is asked by a patient to fill a prescription for a medication that the pharmacist personally believes is not the most appropriate choice, though it is not contraindicated or unsafe for the patient. What is the most appropriate action?
rationale: A pharmacist's personal preference for a different, non-contraindicated therapeutic choice does not justify refusing to fill an otherwise safe, appropriate prescription; professional communication with the prescriber is appropriate if the pharmacist has a genuine clinical concern, but not unilateral refusal based on preference alone.

options.label: A
options.text: Refuse to fill the prescription based on personal preference

options.label: B
options.text: Fill the prescription as written, since it is not unsafe or contraindicated, potentially discussing the pharmacist's clinical perspective with the prescriber if appropriate

options.label: C
options.text: Fill the prescription but intentionally use a less effective generic

options.label: D
options.text: Contact the patient's insurance company to deny coverage

stem: A patient with osteoporosis has been taking an oral bisphosphonate for 5 years. Her physician is considering a "drug holiday." Which of the following best explains the rationale for this practice?
rationale: Bisphosphonates have a prolonged residual effect on bone due to their incorporation into bone matrix, allowing consideration of a temporary treatment pause after extended use to balance ongoing fracture protection against the small but real long-term risks (atypical femur fracture, osteonecrosis of the jaw) associated with prolonged continuous use.

options.label: A
options.text: Bisphosphonates lose all efficacy after 5 years

options.label: B
options.text: Bisphosphonates have a residual effect on bone matrix, allowing consideration of a temporary pause to reduce long-term risks like atypical femur fracture while some benefit persists

options.label: C
options.text: A drug holiday is required by law after 5 years of use

options.label: D
options.text: Drug holidays are only relevant for injectable, not oral, bisphosphonates

stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of Tall Man lettering on medication labels?
rationale: Tall Man lettering capitalizes the distinguishing letters within two look-alike/sound-alike drug names, making the visual distinction more apparent and reducing the chance of misreading one drug for another during a quick visual scan.

options.label: A
options.text: To indicate the medication's therapeutic class

options.label: B
options.text: To visually distinguish look-alike/sound-alike drug names and reduce selection errors

options.label: C
options.text: To indicate controlled substance status

options.label: D
options.text: To show the medication's expiration date more clearly

stem: A 68-year-old man with BPH is being considered for combination therapy given a significantly enlarged prostate on exam. Which combination is most appropriate to address both the static and dynamic components of his obstruction?
rationale: Alpha-1 blockers address the dynamic (smooth muscle tone) component with rapid onset, while 5-alpha reductase inhibitors address the static (prostate size) component by actually shrinking tissue over months — combining both addresses each obstruction mechanism, particularly relevant in a patient with significant prostate enlargement.

options.label: A
options.text: Two different alpha-1 blockers

options.label: B
options.text: An alpha-1 blocker plus a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor

options.label: C
options.text: Two different 5-alpha reductase inhibitors

options.label: D
options.text: A PDE5 inhibitor alone

stem: A study finds a statistically significant difference between two treatments (p<0.05), but the 95% confidence interval for the absolute risk difference includes zero. How should this result be interpreted?
rationale: A 95% confidence interval crossing the null value (zero, for an absolute difference measure) indicates the result is not statistically significant — this would actually be inconsistent with a p<0.05 claim, highlighting the importance of checking whether reported statistics are internally consistent rather than accepting an isolated claim at face value.

options.label: A
options.text: The result is definitively clinically significant

options.label: B
options.text: This is an inconsistent, contradictory finding requiring the study to be discarded entirely

options.label: C
options.text: A confidence interval including zero (the null value for an absolute difference) indicates a non-significant result, regardless of an isolated statement about a p-value

options.label: D
options.text: The p-value should always be trusted over the confidence interval

stem: A pharmacist is asked to combine two IV medications in the same infusion line for a patient with limited IV access. What should be confirmed before proceeding?
rationale: Y-site compatibility must be confirmed against a reliable reference before combining any two IV medications in the same line, given the risk of physical (precipitation) or chemical (degradation) incompatibility — this should never be assumed safe by default.

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing further is needed if both drugs are individually FDA-approved

options.label: B
options.text: Y-site compatibility should be confirmed against a reliable reference before combining the two medications

options.label: C
options.text: The two medications can always be safely combined if given at different rates

options.label: D
options.text: Compatibility is only a concern for oral medications, not IV

stem: A pharmacy technician wants to independently verify a completed prescription's clinical appropriateness (drug, dose, and directions) before it is given to the patient. What is the most appropriate response regarding this scope of practice question?
rationale: Pharmacist clinical judgment functions, including final verification of clinical appropriateness, generally remain a pharmacist responsibility, though technician scope varies meaningfully by state and is expanding in some jurisdictions to include specific, defined verification roles — this is a genuinely state-dependent scope-of-practice question, not a fixed universal answer.

options.label: A
options.text: This is always appropriate regardless of state regulations, since it saves time

options.label: B
options.text: Whether this is appropriate depends on the specific state's regulations, since final clinical verification generally remains a pharmacist responsibility, though some states have expanded technician verification roles in defined circumstances

options.label: C
options.text: Technicians can never participate in any verification step under any circumstances

options.label: D
options.text: This decision is solely at the discretion of the pharmacy's corporate policy, regardless of state law

stem: A patient with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy is started on lactulose. What is the therapeutic target for dosing this medication?
rationale: Lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy is titrated to a target of approximately 2-3 soft stools per day, reflecting adequate colonic acidification and ammonia trapping/elimination without producing excessive, poorly-tolerated diarrhea.

options.label: A
options.text: Complete cessation of bowel movements

options.label: B
options.text: 2 to 3 soft stools per day

options.label: C
options.text: At least 6 watery stools per day

options.label: D
options.text: A fixed dose regardless of clinical response

stem: An 88-year-old man with dementia living in a long-term care facility develops new agitation and aggressive behavior. The facility physician is considering starting an antipsychotic. What is the most important consideration before proceeding?
rationale: Antipsychotics carry a boxed warning for increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis, making non-pharmacologic approaches the generally preferred first-line strategy for behavioral symptoms, with antipsychotic use reserved for more limited, carefully considered circumstances.

options.label: A
options.text: Antipsychotics are first-line and should be started immediately for any dementia-related agitation

options.label: B
options.text: Non-pharmacologic approaches should generally be tried first, given the boxed warning for increased mortality with antipsychotic use in dementia-related psychosis/behavioral symptoms

options.label: C
options.text: There is no specific safety concern with antipsychotic use in this population

options.label: D
options.text: A higher dose should be used to ensure rapid symptom control

stem: A pediatric patient weighing 18 kg requires a medication dosed at 15 mg/kg/day, divided into 3 equal doses. What is the dose per administration, in mg? Round to the nearest whole number.
rationale: Total daily dose = 18 kg × 15 mg/kg/day = 270 mg/day. Divided into 3 equal doses: 270 / 3 = 90 mg per dose.

stem: A patient is prescribed a gravity IV infusion of 1000 mL to run over 8 hours, using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What is the correct infusion rate in gtt/min? Round to the nearest whole number.
rationale: Rate (gtt/min) = (volume × drop factor) / (time in minutes) = (1000 mL × 15 gtt/mL) / (480 min) ≈ 31 gtt/min.

stem: A patient receiving TPN develops signs of catheter-related bloodstream infection. Which of the following is most directly relevant to this specific complication of long-term parenteral nutrition?
rationale: Long-term parenteral nutrition requires sustained central venous access, creating an ongoing infection risk requiring careful catheter care technique — catheter-related bloodstream infection is a specific, recognized complication tied directly to this required access route, distinct from TPN's metabolic complications.

options.label: A
options.text: Hyperglycemia from dextrose content

options.label: B
options.text: The central venous access required for TPN administration over an extended period

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatic complications from prolonged use

options.label: D
options.text: Electrolyte imbalance from the formulation

stem: A patient presents to the emergency department after an intentional overdose of an unknown quantity of aspirin approximately 3 hours ago. Initial labs show a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis pattern. Which of the following is an appropriate component of management?
rationale: Salicylate toxicity produces a classic mixed respiratory alkalosis/metabolic acidosis picture; urinary alkalinization with IV sodium bicarbonate promotes ion trapping of salicylate in the urine, enhancing elimination — a mechanism-based intervention distinct from simple supportive care, with hemodialysis reserved for more severe cases.

options.label: A
options.text: Urinary acidification to trap the drug in the kidney

options.label: B
options.text: Urinary alkalinization to enhance renal elimination via ion trapping

options.label: C
options.text: Naloxone administration

options.label: D
options.text: Immediate hemodialysis regardless of severity

stem: A 79-year-old man with a normal-appearing serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL is being considered for a renally-cleared medication requiring dose adjustment based on calculated creatinine clearance. He weighs 62 kg and has significantly reduced muscle mass due to age-related sarcopenia. What is the most important consideration in this scenario?
rationale: Serum creatinine depends on muscle mass for its production; an older adult with reduced muscle mass can have a "normal-looking" creatinine despite significantly reduced actual renal function — calculated CrCl (Cockcroft-Gault, incorporating age and weight) accounts for this and should guide dosing rather than creatinine alone.

options.label: A
options.text: His serum creatinine alone is sufficient to guide dosing

options.label: B
options.text: His serum creatinine may significantly underestimate true renal impairment given his reduced muscle mass, and a calculated CrCl should be used instead

options.label: C
options.text: No dose adjustment is needed since his creatinine is within normal range

options.label: D
options.text: His age alone, without any calculation, should determine the dose
